item.title: Ada-Calvo administration to open government positions to public applicants

item.content:encoded:
Gov.-elect Tony Ada and Lt. Gov.-elect E.J. Calvo said their incoming administration will open cabinet and senior staff positions to public applicants, with an emphasis on professional experience, qualifications, and commitment to public service rather than political affiliation.

During their first press conference as governor and lieutenant governor-elect, the two outlined plans to establish an online application portal where interested residents, including current government employees, can submit resumes and apply for positions within the incoming administration.

Jadeen Perez, who will chair the transition team’s Committee on Administration and Appointees, said the committee plans to begin accepting applications after the election results are certified on Nov. 19.

Applicants will undergo background checks and an evaluation of their qualifications before the committee submits recommendations to Ada and Calvo.

Ada said the application process will be open to anyone interested in serving, including members of the current administration.

“The bottom line is, everybody working together, regardless of party affiliation,” Ada said. “Election is over. Now it’s time for everybody to come together and work together.”

The incoming administration has also established three principal transition committees to guide the transfer of government responsibilities. The Committee on Government Operations and Efficiency, chaired by Nate Denight, will review the operations of government agencies, identify opportunities to improve efficiency, and assess existing challenges. The Committee on Administration and Appointees will oversee the recruitment and evaluation of potential cabinet members and senior staff, while the Committee on Inaugural Arrangements, chaired by Piti Mayor Jesse Alig, will coordinate inauguration preparations.

Denight said the government operations committee will establish additional subcommittees to review the island’s 52 government agencies. The committees will meet with agency management and staff to identify what is working, what needs improvement, and what resources may be needed.

Their findings will be compiled into a final transition report outlining each department’s current situation, objectives, and recommendations. Transition chair Jerry Crisostomo said the report will help Ada and Calvo determine their administration’s priorities and guide appointments ahead of their expected Jan. 4 start in office.

Ada said the incoming administration will first focus on completing a smooth transition and assessing the government’s financial position and operational needs before determining its immediate priorities.

One policy direction the incoming administration has already identified is a dedicated executive leadership position for tourism and destination development, separate from economic development. Calvo said they may be the first administration ever to dedicate an executive position to the industry of tourism.

“The position we’re looking at is actually tourism and destination development, separate from economic development, which is important,” Calvo said, “I think that would probably have fallen under economic development in the past, but we need to look at diversifying our economy and also protecting other growing industries separately.”

Ada said the position would reflect tourism’s significant impact on Guam’s economy and employment, particularly as the island’s tourism industry continues to face challenges.

When asked about their first 100 days in office, Ada said the administration will begin implementing its campaign plans after evaluating the government’s needs and establishing its leadership team. Calvo identified tourism, economic development, federal relations, and education as among the areas that will require attention.

When asked what the new administration is most excited to begin working on as they work toward a smooth government transition, they said they plan to continue monthly community cleanups, which began during the campaign.

“We want to still get out there and keep our community clean,” Ada said. “We want to ensure that, as we continue to move along within the first 100 days of our administration, that we start implementing our plans and get it to what we said during our campaign. You’re going to start seeing the implementation of those plans come to fruition.”

Ada and Calvo said they will seek guidance from former Republican governors and lieutenant governors to assist with the transition. Those invited to serve as honorary transition advisers include former governors Felix Camacho and Eddie Calvo, along with former lieutenant governors Ray Tenorio, Mike Cruz and Kaleo Moylan.

The transition team says additional appointments and opportunities for public participation will be announced in the coming weeks. Updates are expected through the incoming administration’s website and social media platforms.

item.title: CNMI runoff elections set for Nov. 20 after certification
item.description: The Commonwealth Election Commission is expected to certify the results of the 2026 general election Friday, formally triggering a 14-day countdown to runoff elections on Nov. 20 for governor and attorney general, according to CEC Executive Director Kayla Igitol Magofna. Magofna said Thursday that election commissioners are scheduled to certify the official results, setting into motion preparation
item.content:encoded:
The Commonwealth Election Commission is expected to certify the results of the 2026 general election Friday, formally triggering a 14-day countdown to runoff elections on Nov. 20 for governor and attorney general, according to CEC Executive Director Kayla Igitol Magofna.

Magofna said Thursday that election commissioners are scheduled to certify the official results, setting into motion preparations for the runoff election required under CNMI law when no candidate secures more than 50% of all votes cast and counted.

"So we have to have an election 14 days after," Magofna said.

The certification will finalize results from the Nov. 3 general election and establish the timeline for distributing runoff ballots and preparing polling sites across the Commonwealth.

According to the CEC, absentee voters who requested ballots for the general election will automatically receive absentee ballots for the runoff election. Election officials said no new requests for overseas absentee ballots will be accepted, although over-the-counter absentee voting will remain available.

Earlier, the commission mailed out 1,420 absentee ballots for the general election. Election officials counted 886 absentee ballots in the final tabulation and noted that ballots had to be received on Saipan on or before Election Day to be included in the certified results.

For the runoff election, the commission said it will continue to receive absentee ballots for up to 14 days after Election Day pursuant to its established procedures.

The certified results are expected to confirm runoff contests in both the governor's and attorney general's races.

In the gubernatorial contest, the Republican ticket of Ralph DLG Torres and Benjamin Jones Jr. led the field with 6,437 votes, or 49.5% of ballots cast, narrowly missing the majority needed to avoid a runoff. The independent ticket of Blas Jonathan Attao and Edmund Villagomez finished second with 5,043 votes, or 38.7%, advancing to the Nov. 20 runoff.

The independent team of Lawrence F. Camacho and Edith Deleon Guerrero placed third with 1,537 votes, or 11.8%.

The attorney general race also failed to produce a majority winner. Attorney Joaquin DLG Torres received 5,073 votes, or 39.7%, while attorney Michael Evangelista secured 3,854 votes, or 30.2%. Attorney Jonathan Robert Glass Jr. followed closely with 3,836 votes, or 30.1%.

Under CNMI law, the top two vote-getters advance to a runoff when no gubernatorial candidate or attorney general candidate receives more than half of all votes cast and counted.

The Commonwealth had 18,521 registered voters for the 2026 election. More than 13,000 voters cast ballots in the gubernatorial race, leaving roughly 5,500 registered voters who did not participate.

Election officials said registered voters who did not vote in the general election remain eligible to cast ballots in the Nov. 20 runoff election.

With certification anticipated Friday, election administrators will have two weeks to complete preparations for what is expected to be a closely watched runoff that will determine the Commonwealth's next governor and attorney general.

item.content:encoded:
The 39 th Guam Legislature will bring new faces, as well as some returning senators, into Guam’s lawmaking body.

A number of senators in the 38 th Guam Legislature gave up their seats to run for higher office. Republican Speaker Frank Blas Jr., Republican Vice Speaker Tony Ada and Democratic Sens. Therese Terlaje and Joe San Agustin all ran for governor, with Ada winning the island’s highest office.

Democratic Sens. Sabina Perez and Tina Muna Barnes ran for lieutenant governor.

That left nine incumbents, all of whom won reelection.

They are Republicans Sabrina Salas Matanane, Jesse Lujan, Chris Duenas, Shelly Calvo, Telo Taitague, Vincent Borja and Eulogio Shawn Gumatatao. Democratic incumbents reelected were Chris Barnett and William Parkinson.

Former Democratic Sens. Amanda Shelton, Telena Nelson and Clynton Ridgell were elected Tuesday, along with Democratic legislative newcomers Donna Quinata and Kallen Perez.

Hoa Nyugen is the Republican newcomer, giving the party an 8-7 majority in the 39 th Legislature.

item.title: Low birth rates were emptying public schools. ICE deportations are now making it worse
item.description: Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly. LOS ANGELES — Long before the Trump administration started deporting hundreds of thousands of immigrants, many with school-age children, public schools nationwide faced a massive and accelerating drop in student enrollment caused mostly by shrinking families.
item.content:encoded:
Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.

LOS ANGELES — Long before the Trump administration started deporting hundreds of thousands of immigrants, many with school-age children, public schools nationwide faced a massive and accelerating drop in student enrollment caused mostly by shrinking families.

"Birth rates here in Los Angeles County have been declining for decades, which means fewer children enrolled in our schools," said Kelly Gonez, a board member in the LA Unified School District (LAUSD), the second largest in the country, which lost more than 300,000 students over the last two decades.

LA isn't alone. The population of children under age 18 began to fall nationwide after 2010, according to U.S. Census data , dropping by roughly 2.1 million kids through 2025 .

With public schools in much of the country facing a demographic cliff, the Trump administration last year began detaining and expelling large numbers of foreign residents. A study by the Migration Policy Institute found as many as 1.9 million people left the U.S. during the first 18 months of Trump's second term.

As part of the crackdown effort, federal officials weakened restrictions that prevented ICE agents from operating near public schools. "Many of our families immediately went into hiding," Gonez said. "We were predicting a 2% drop in enrollment. It was double that."

Researchers who study education and population trends aren't surprised. This is the first time in nearly a century, since the era of the Great Depression, that birth rates and immigration levels are low at the same time. Large-scale deportations mean even bigger and more rapid changes in areas with large immigrant communities.

"The U.S. isn't alone in facing the challenges of demographic decline," said Thomas Dee, an economist who specializes in education policy at Stanford University. "To stop or slow immigration really exacerbates those problems. Communities are now confronting very painful decisions about closing schools."

The scale of decline is daunting. According to the U.S Department of Education , the number of kids in public schools nationwide peaked in 2019 and fell by roughly 1.5 million students as of the 2024 school year.

Based on data gathered before Trump's immigration crackdown began, federal researchers project enrollment will decline by at least another 2 million students by 2030. That would mean a 7% national decline in roughly a decade.

It's unclear how large or sustained the impact of Trump-era immigration policies will be on enrollment trends. Dee and other researchers say that depends on how long ICE crackdowns and other restrictions remain in place.

In the short term, the blow to many districts could be severe. When Dee studied public schools in communities hit by ICE raids in California's Central Valley in 2025, he found student daily absences spiked more than 20% .

Texas, meanwhile, saw the number of kids in classrooms plunge statewide last year by more than 76,000 students. The vast majority of that drop came among Hispanic kids and the children of immigrant families, according to a study by the Texas Education Agency .

Florida, home to a large community of Haitian refugees who were stripped of temporary protected status by the Trump administration in July, saw a big drop in enrollment this year. The state's two largest public school districts, Miami-Dade and Broward County , lost roughly 30,000 children combined in a single year.

"It's really the effect of both the exodus of the existing families and stopping the inflow [of foreign migrants and children] that normally would have occurred," Dee said.

A report published in June by two education think tanks, Bellwether and WestEd , warned that public schools have entered an era of "sustained" enrollment declines which are already reshaping districts in 40 states.

The analysis found the "primary overall driver of declining enrollment is a sustained drop in birth rates" followed by a "national slowdown in immigration."

"At the local level, enrollment decline may permanently reduce available resources and will significantly reshape public education systems for years to come," the study concluded, while predicting a loss of $11 billion a year in public school funding linked to falling enrollment.

Other factors have spurred public school enrollment losses, including the COVID-19 pandemic and the shift of more students to private and homeschool learning. But the U.S. Department of Education projects private schools, too, will lose more than a million students by the end of this decade.

While debates over immigration policy play out in Washington, D.C., teachers, parents and students say ICE crackdowns already mean more empty classrooms and less vibrant neighborhoods around schools.

"This street right here is actually where the ICE standoff happened. It was right before school," said teacher Guadalupe Cardona, who stood recently outside Santee Education Complex, a high school in South Los Angeles as school buses rumbled past.

In October 2025, an ICE agent opened fire here. No children or school employees were injured, but a man from Mexico without legal status and an ICE agent were struck by bullets. Cardona believes fear following that clash and other raids caused enrollment to plummet.

"In my school alone, we had over 200 students that didn't show up on the first day of school," she said.

"We found that a lot of them were just [gone], no longer living where they had put their address down. We lost two teachers at the beginning of the school year because of it. It is something that hurts beyond just, like, putting your job at risk."

Guadalupe Pineda, a parent, works in a shop just down the street from Santee High. She says dread of ICE, combined with fewer students coming and going, have hurt her community. "There's definitely less sales, less traffic, less everything."

After growing up in LA and attending public school here without legal status, Pineda told NPR she was able to secure U.S. citizenship a few years ago. She said she understands why people are pulling their kids out of school and in many cases leaving the U.S. altogether.

"People are still scared, very much scared to go out to do everyday things. I feel like if I didn't have everything set [with my immigration status], I would probably leave. I would be afraid of being separated from my family."

NPR asked White House officials about the impact on public schools of ICE crackdowns and other federal immigration policies, including the revocation of temporary refugee status for hundreds of thousands of people living in the U.S. legally.

White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis sent a brief email response saying deportations "make American classrooms less crowded." Bis also pointed to a September post on the social media platform X, where administration officials celebrated the overall drop in the number of legal and undocumented immigrants living in the U.S.

"The total foreign-born population declined 2.9 million from January 2025 to July 2026," the statement said . "The huge recent decline in the foreign-born population indicates that net migration to the United States was negative in the last year and a half for the first time since the 1930s."

item.title: After cancer surgery, Pope Leo embarks on Latin America trip

item.content:encoded:
ROME — Pope Leo XIV is kicking off a three-nation tour of Latin America with a visit to Uruguay, the region's least Catholic and most secular country, three weeks after undergoing lung cancer surgery that had put the entire trip into question.

Leo is due to arrive in Montevideo after a 13-and-a-half hour flight from Rome. He has a packed three-day itinerary in Uruguay including a visit to a neighborhood plagued by gang violence, a Mass in Paysandú, some 375 kilometers (230 miles) from the capital, and another Mass in the city of Florida, about 100 kilometers (60 miles) away.

The Uruguay leg is the first stop on what will be the longest and farthest trip of his pontificate, all being undertaken as the 71-year-old pope continues his recovery. The trip will also bring him to neighboring Argentina and finally back home to Peru, where Leo served as a missionary priest and bishop for two decades.

"His stamina is fantastic. The way that he's singing is incredible. And you can only sing if your lungs are really strong," said Maria Montserrat Alvar, the Vatican's new communications chief. She noted that Leo has passed the 14-day convalescence period required by doctors after his Oct. 13 surgery and is eager to get on the road.

"His doctors are very confident and he'll have plenty of medical care on board should something happen, but we don't see that in his prognosis or even in the way that he's acting," she said.

In Uruguay, which hasn't had a papal visit since 1988, Leo is expected to try to remind the 3.5 million people of their strong Catholic heritage stemming from the times of Spanish colonial rule. He is likely to propose the faith anew as an answer to today's challenges and problems.

Upon arrival, Leo will meet with President Yamandú Orsi, leader of the center-left alliance that assumed power in Uruguay in March 2025, and then deliver his welcome address to government officials and diplomats. He finishes the long day with a vespers service at the city's cathedral.

Leo will find in Uruguay a country unlike any other in Latin America, which is home to around 40% of the world's 1.4 billion Catholics. Uruguay is considered the most secular country in the region, where only a fraction of people who identify as Catholic actually go to Mass regularly.

Uruguay was the first country in the world to legalize marijuana for recreational use, the second country in Latin America to decriminalize abortion, and the third country in the Americas to legalize same-sex marriage.

More recently, it became the first country in the region to approve assisted dying legislation over the strong opposition of the Catholic Church, evidence of Uruguay's entrenched, church-state separation that prohibits any mention of God in oaths of office.

Leo is expected to recall the church's opposition to abortion and euthanasia as part of his broader argument about upholding human dignity in all phases of life.

Uruguayan church officials have marveled at the apparent enthusiasm the visit has provoked, with reports that tickets to Leo's prayer vigil at Montevideo's Centenario Stadium were snapped up after two days.

"It seems that the pope's presence is shifting something here and is gradually breaking down this veil that has always sought to obscure and diminish the presence of the Catholic tradition that lies at the country's foundation," said Guzmán Carriquiry, the Uruguayan former head of the Vatican's pontifical commission for Latin America.

"I believe this pope will stir up questions in the hearts of Uruguayans -- disturbing questions -- questions about meaning and, we hope, questions about faith," he said.

Carriquiry said he expects Leo will seek to revive the Catholic roots of Uruguay, especially when he travels to Florida on Sunday to mark an important Catholic feast day.

The Nov. 8 feast commemorates the Virgin of the Thirty-three, a small wooden icon of the Virgin Mary that is intricately connected to Uruguay's independence movement. According to tradition, 33 independence patriots acquired the Guaraní statue and had it with them when independence was declared from the Brazilian empire in Florida on Aug. 25, 1825.

"So the number 33 is an ecclesiastical symbol, a national symbol," said Carriquiry, who was also Uruguay's ambassador to the Holy See. "And so the pope will speak there about the Catholic tradition that lies at the origin of Uruguay—that stems from Uruguay and gave rise to Uruguay—in order to revive and renew the Catholic tradition in the hearts of Uruguayans."

Andrew Chesnut, chair of Catholic studies and an expert in the Latin American church at Virginia Commonwealth University, said he wasn't surprised that Leo's visit had generated enthusiasm and that he will be welcomed warmly.

"But that's not necessarily going to translate into folks in the pews," he said. "If the overarching goal is trying to revitalize Catholicism in the most Catholic region on Earth, Uruguay is kind of a lost cause, and it has been for decades."

item.title: A judge blocks construction of Trump's arch moments after it won federal approval
item.description: Updated November 6, 2026 at 7:50 PM ChST A federal judge blocked construction of President Trump's arch, stopping work the administration had hoped to begin immediately.
item.content:encoded:
Updated November 6, 2026 at 7:50 PM ChST

A federal judge blocked construction of President Trump's arch, stopping work the administration had hoped to begin immediately.

Just before midnight Friday, District Court Judge Tanya Chutkan issued an order — finalized and made public minutes later - barring the government from any construction work for 14 days, granting a request filed days earlier by the governments of D.C. and Virginia .

She laid out her reasoning in a 33-page opinion , in which she scrutinized the administration's competing justifications for the arch — particularly its sudden emphasis on national security — and agreed that the local governments are likely to be harmed by its construction. The 250-foot arch would stand in Memorial Circle, a traffic island on the bridge linking the Lincoln Memorial to Arlington National Cemetery.

Trump administration officials have said work would take place 20 hours a day, year-round, for two to three years. In addition to questioning the arch's legality, D.C. and Virginia argue the construction would cause all sorts of financial and logistical disruptions.

"The threatened harms will materialize as soon as construction begins, in part because the traffic disruptions will occur immediately," Chutkan agreed.

Chutkan's ruling came less than two hours after a federal planning commission packed with presidential allies granted final approval to the arch in an 8-4 vote. The National Capital Planning Commission heard nearly eight hours of impassioned pleas from veterans, lawmakers, residents and concerned citizens opposed to the structure.

The Trump administration had previously told the court it could begin excavation work that same day, despite lacking authorization from Congress and an expanding legal challenge.

A group of Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian sued the government earlier this year, arguing that an arch is unlawful without Congressional approval, which the administration has not sought. The Democratic governments of D.C. and Virginia jointly filed a similar lawsuit last weekend.

Chutkan consolidated the lawsuits and asked the government to notify the court within an hour of commission approval, setting the stage for an 11th-hour ruling.

Thursday started with a protest on Memorial Circle, where dozens of people spoke against the arch. The grass underfoot was already marked with white paint. Lawyers for the government told the court in a midday filing that the lines were painted on Saturday by its designated construction firm, seemingly without authorization from the National Park Service.

The commission meeting began at 1 p.m. It was held virtually because of the high volume of public testimony: 131 people were signed up to speak.

Just minutes into public testimony, the livestream crashed, lengthening the meeting by about an hour until it was restored. Over the course of nearly nine hours, commissioners heard from dozens of veterans and their relatives, Democratic lawmakers, historic preservation experts and concerned citizens from D.C. and beyond.

Among their many concerns , critics said the structure would obstruct an important view , insult service members buried on the hallowed ground of nearby Arlington National Cemetery and add a layer of risk to the notoriously complicated D.C. airspace. They have questions about its legality and its cost, which the administration has not confirmed.

Many see the arch as part of Trump's unilateral effort to memorialize himself in the nation's capital — and described Democrats' midterm sweep as a referendum against it.

"Leaving aside all of the legitimate concerns and challenges about the required approvals, funding, land use, single-source bidding, and peer review, the American people spoke this past Tuesday at the ballot box," said former D.C. resident Emi Yamauchi. "They said enough vanity projects, enough corruption, enough Reflecting Pool travesties."

Only a handful of speakers offered support for the arch, including Republican Reps. Andrew Clyde of Georgia and Brian Mast of Florida, both of whom are veterans.

Much of the night's testimony was heartfelt and personal: Many speakers had family members buried — or plans for their own future burials — at Arlington National Cemetery. Several implored the commissioners not to ruin their reputations by recording their support for the arch.

"[These are] warnings about the threat your own behavior poses to your political power, your moral authority, the legacy you leave to your descendants, and your eternal souls," said Stephen Eubank, some seven hours into the public testimony.

As the night wore on, a few speakers even questioned whether the commissioners — who were not shown on screen — were even listening. Many suggested the approval was a foregone conclusion, noting the political makeup of the commission and the fact that Trump-appointed Chair Mark Paoletta and several other members had expressed their support for the arch at the start of the meeting.

The commission started deliberating just before 10 p.m. The discussion lasted less than an hour.

The commissioners who spoke first were Trump allies and appointees. They thanked the speakers for taking the time to share their views, but — in brief comments — expressed their support for moving forward. They continued to cast the arch as a tribute to the nation and those who served, despite the broad pushback from individual veterans and veterans' groups .

The Trump allies dismissed concerns that the arch would violate D.C.'s restrictions on building heights as well as federal environmental and historic preservation laws . They maintained that Congress authorized the project when it approved a pair of 166-foot columns on Memorial Circle in 1925, which were never built.

And they pointed to recent claims by Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth that the monument will enhance national security — even though officials at the meeting confirmed that no such analysis or details were included in the final submission. In fact, Interior Department official Greg Wischer said "specific national security functions have been filed under seal" in court but that the National Park Service "has not been privy to any national defense preparations."

The most vocal criticism of the arch came from D.C. Council Chair Phil Mendelson, a Democrat who sits on the council. He asked questions about the arch's purpose — military and otherwise — earlier in the meeting and said, during deliberations, that he was dissatisfied with the government's contradictory answers.

"We cannot approve final site and building plans until we have the final site and building plan," Mendelson said. He introduced a motion to postpone the vote until those plans could be submitted, or until the commission's next meeting in early December. The motion failed by a vote of 4 to 8.

Vice Chair Stuart Levenbach, a Trump appointee, expressed concerns about delaying the vote because the "project proponent is under a time constraint and wants the decision today," suggesting the government wants to "commence building very quickly."

Within minutes, the commission had given the arch its green light. The Trump administration notified the court within half an hour. By Friday, that light had turned red — at least temporarily.

"While this decision prevents Donald Trump from immediately implementing his plans to create a monument to his own ego, the courts and Congress must put in place permanent safeguards to stop the Trump Administration from violating the law and proceeding with this project," Rep. Don Beyer, a Virginia Democrat, said in a statement.

Historic preservation groups wasted no time slamming both the process and the outcome.
